findings.where: First screen, Mark's photograph (desktop right half; phone, above the line), and the grade the Texture section describes
findings.fault: The direction is 'Mark at work': one full-bleed photograph of him speaking, graded into the house colours, with his line set over its calm side. This build keys out the photograph's backdrop instead and fills it with flat slate. What is left is a cut-out of his head and shoulders on a flat navy field, not a photograph in real light. The lectern and the event are gone, apart from the tip of a microphone. On the phone the cut-out ends at the collar and reads as a floating head above the heading. The first screen ends up as a portrait on a dark ground, which is what v4 and v6 already cover, and v7's own lever is lost.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for v7 to be the full-bleed 'Mark at work' direction and judges the first screen first. Bank and agency staff would also lose the sense that a real person works in real rooms, which the research's 'real people in real light' is there to give them.

findings.where: Texture section, the stated grading method ('a new photograph on a flat backdrop takes the same grade')
findings.fault: The look depends on keying out a flat backdrop. The photographs this site needs most are of Mark at named events, like the busy Belt and Road interview used in the article. Those have no flat backdrop, so the method can't make the hero from any of them. The image round would be limited to studio-style shots, or would break the look.
findings.who_objects: The founder and the image round, which plan to refresh images from Mark's events and LinkedIn posts. The trust checklist also asks for a photo at a named event, and this hero treatment can't hold one.

findings.where: Article specimen, the numbers on the three-item list
findings.fault: The list numbers are set in the house blue. The page uses that colour only for links and the action, and the article's own side note says 'blue only where something can be clicked'. The numbers are static text that has borrowed the link colour.
findings.who_objects: A reader who has learned on this page that blue means clickable would see the blue numbers as links. Angélique would also copy the contradiction into every article she builds.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture row at the article's end ('Streamlining the PPP Process…', PDF with a download arrow)
findings.fault: The row promises a direct PDF download, but the parts map shows its link goes to #article. The row also has no heading, so nothing says why a 2026 lecture follows a 2024 blog post: it isn't marked as related or as the next item. The house pattern is a PDF behind an HTML page for each talk, not a bare download.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader looking for Mark's talks: the download label doesn't do what it says, and without a heading they can't tell what this list is.

findings.where: Navigation: Profile, Articles and talks, Blog
findings.fault: All three nav links go to the same place (#article), so 'Profile' opens a blog article. 'Articles and talks' and 'Blog' also overlap: the specimen article is labelled 'Blog No. 8', so a visitor can't tell which of the two holds Mark's writing.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank visitor who clicks Profile for his background and lands in an essay, or who has to guess between two links for his publications.

findings.where: First screen, the 'Placeholder…' photo caption (desktop bottom left; phone below the action)
findings.fault: The caption belongs to the photograph but sits at the far left under the action on desktop, and below the action on the phone. Placed there, it reads as small print about the email offer, not as a note on the photo.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the first screen: the stand-in label is meant to sit clearly with the image it qualifies.

findings.where: Header, 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the logo
findings.fault: The name leads the lockup in the bright text colour but does nothing when clicked. Only the logo beside it goes home, against the common pattern where the site owner's name is the home link.
findings.who_objects: A visitor on a deep page who clicks the name to get home and gets no response.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best…', and 'Mark's voice' in the Type pair section
findings.fault: These use straight apostrophes, while the rest of the page uses curly quotes (‘chapter topics’, “Not yet!”, Mark’s in the footer).
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of a legal-journal-style page, for whom mixed quote marks look unedited. The display size of the title makes it easy to spot.
